wsl-claude: yes, and multiplexing with a max frame is exactly what fixes the relay problem I raised. Every stream and every ordinary message is cut into frames no bigger than the max, and the connection takes turns between them. A small message then waits at most one frame, never behind a whole photo, and the relay's fairness becomes 'one frame per stream per turn' instead of 'one message per target'. The max frame is also the memory bound: the relay never holds more than a frame per stream.
One alternative worth weighing before building our own framing over WebSocket: HTTP/2 already IS this, with streams, frames, a max frame size, per-stream flow control and taking turns, all built in. Node has it (the http2 module), and Caddy, which fronts the relay, already speaks it. WebSocket gives one plain pipe and we'd write the multiplexing ourselves; HTTP/2 gives the multiplexing and we'd only decide the rules. Both are worth a look in the goal; I'd start from HTTP/2.
the relay a ticker that synchronizes internal stream packets, among peer streams for fairness
the relay a ticker that synchronizes internal stream packets, among peer streams for fairness

Yes, that's the relay's whole job in this design: a ticker. Each tick, it forwards one frame from every active stream in turn, so no peer's stream can starve another's. And the ticker gives you control almost for free: frames per tick times the frame size is the relay's bandwidth, so a relay owner can set how much the box gives, and share it evenly among the streams going through it.

wsl-claude: yes, the relay as the scheduler of frames. Two refinements so the ticker is fair AND fast:
1) A TURN, NOT A CLOCK. If it ticks at a fixed rate, the line sits idle whenever only one stream is running. Better: each round, forward one frame from every stream that has one ready, then start the next round at once. With one stream it runs at full speed; with ten, each gets a tenth.
2) FAIR BETWEEN MEMBERS, NOT STREAMS. If the turns go stream by stream, a member who opens 50 streams gets 50 times the share of one who opens one. So take turns between MEMBERS first, then between that member's own streams. That matches today's rule, which is per requester and per target (router.js:27, :48), and keeps one heavy user from starving the relay.
Both are easy to test: two members, one with 50 streams and one with 1, get equal throughput; a lone stream runs at line speed.

wsl-claude: claude-windows' point is good: the tick gives the relay owner a bandwidth dial. We can have both: the owner sets a CEILING (frames per second the box will give), and within it the relay runs turn by turn, members first, then each member's streams. Under the ceiling nothing waits for a clock, so a lone stream gets the whole allowance at once; at the ceiling, the allowance is split evenly between members. One setting the owner understands (how much this box gives), and fairness that holds whether one person or fifty are streaming.

and if multiplexed the would be merge and fan concepts
and if multiplexed the would be merge and fan concepts

Yes, the two directions of the same frames. MERGE: many streams into one connection, which is the multiplexing itself (a node's uploads, chats and files share one link). FAN: one stream out to many receivers. The sender uploads each frame once, and the relay copies it to every subscriber on its turn (a live video to ten viewers costs the sender one upload, not ten). Both use the same frames and the same turn-taking, so fan-out needs no new mechanism, only a stream that has more than one receiver.
